name: XAD
baseline: CppAD, Adept 2, autodiff (C++ AD libraries), finite differences
workload: Gradient computation (adjoint AD) on four quant-finance kernels: Heston Monte Carlo (10K paths), SABR calibration, XVA CVA, LIBOR swaption.
claimed_speedup: Heston MC: XAD-Codegen 21 ms vs XAD tape 40 ms vs Adept 91 ms; SABR 4.9 ms vs competitors 8.4-38 ms; XAD-Codegen 2x-5x faster than XAD tape mode; adjoint ~70x faster than finite differences on LIBOR (161 inputs)
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 copyleft (commercial license sold separately); tape-based reverse mode uses memory; native-code codegen backend is AVX2-targeted.
caveats: Benchmark repo is the project's own (1 commit, 5 stars, MIT) but code, compiler, flags and CPU are public. Baselines are AD libraries, not oneDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen tensor. autodiff lib completed only one benchmark. Per-library numbers beyond those quoted not individually verified.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ forward-mode automatic differentiation library benchmark faster than Eigen autodiff Stan Adept CppAD

name: FastAD
baseline: Adept, Stan Math, ADOL-C, CppAD, Sacado (C++ AD libraries)
workload: Forward and reverse-mode gradient evaluation of expression-template AD on sum, product, log-sum-exp, matrix ops, normal log-pdf, regression and stochastic-volatility models.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: '2-10 times faster than Adept and 2-19 times faster than Stan across various test cases'; README: 'over orders of magnitude improvement' vs Adept, Stan, ADOL-C, CppAD, Sacado
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17, depends on Eigen 3.3; expression templates and static graph structure limit dynamic control flow.
caveats: Paper abstract gives no hardware/compiler. ADBenchmark repo (https://github.com/JamesYang007/ADBenchmark) says only tested on macOS Catalina with GCC10; flags/CPU not stated, so not tier A. Baselines are AD libraries, not the category baselines.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ forward-mode automatic differentiation library benchmark faster than Eigen autodiff Stan Adept CppAD

name: llamafile tinyBLAS CPU matmul kernels
baseline: llama.cpp CPU matmul (prior kernels); Intel MKL sgemm
workload: LLM prompt-evaluation (prefill) tokens/sec on CPU with F16 and Q8_0 weights; also a raw GEMM GFLOPS comparison vs MKL.
claimed_speedup: 'prompt eval ... anywhere between 30% and 500% faster' with F16/Q8_0; e.g. Mistral 7B f16 on Threadripper 7995WX 485 vs 197 tok/s; TinyLlama f16 on Raspberry Pi 5 62 vs 28 tok/s; 790 GFLOPS on Alderlake vs MKL 295 GFLOPS for the tested matrix size
tradeoffs: Kernels were upstreamed to llama.cpp (MIT); gains target prompt eval, not token generation; disabled by default on Apple M2.
caveats: Author's own blog post; compiler flags not captured; PR https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/6414 reports ~40% on Q4_0/Q8_0 and 2x on F16 with independent user reports. Baseline is llama.cpp, not oneDNN/XNNPACK; the MKL comparison is a single matrix size.
found_via: WebSearch: llamafile tinyBLAS matmul kernels faster than llama.cpp MKL

name: BitNet (bitnet.cpp)
workload: CPU inference of 1.58-bit (ternary) LLMs using lookup-table kernels, measured against full-precision models.
claimed_speedup: 'speedups of 1.37x to 5.07x on ARM CPUs' and '2.37x to 6.17x on x86 CPUs'; energy reduced 55.4%-82.2%; 100B model at 5-7 tokens/s on one CPU
tradeoffs: Requires ternary-trained BitNet b1.58 models; lossless only relative to those models; clang>=18, CMake>=3.22.
caveats: Baseline is the full-precision llama.cpp path on different (higher-bit) weights, so the speedup mixes quantization with kernel gains. Technical report https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16144 not opened. Per-CPU hardware table exists in the README but was not extracted.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ neural network inference kernels (BitNet repo fetched directly)

compiler_and_flags: Clang 17.0.6 on Windows; CMake>=3.22 (flags not stated)
hardware: Surface Laptop 7 (Snapdragon X Elite), M2-Ultra, Jetson AGX Orin, Raspberry Pi 5
name: T-MAC
workload: Low-bit LLM token generation and prefill on CPU using lookup tables instead of dequantize-multiply (BitNet-3B, Llama-2-7B W2/W4).
claimed_speedup: '4~5x speedup compared to SOTA CPU low-bit framework (llama.cpp)' on Surface Laptop 7 (20 tok/s 1 core, 48 tok/s 4 cores for 3B BitNet); matches 40 tok/s with 2 cores vs 8 for llama.cpp
tradeoffs: Needs TVM built from source and Python tooling; low-bit (1-4 bit) weights only.
caveats: First-party numbers against llama.cpp b2794 (May 2024); README notes baseline throughput was unstable under thermal limits so a second 'Best Performance' profile was added. Published as an EuroSys'25 paper (not opened here). Baseline not in the category list.

name: LIBXSMM
workload: Batch-reduce GEMM based LSTM, fully-connected and CNN (ResNet-50) primitives built on LIBXSMM, on Skylake-SP.
claimed_speedup: LSTM forward 1.2-1.3x and backward/update 1.1-1.7x faster than MKL-DNN; fully connected layers 1.16x, 1.36x, 1.09x; ResNet-50 forward efficiency 83% vs 81% (paper abstract, arXiv 1906.06440, SC'19)
tradeoffs: JIT code generation; library ABI or header-only; x86 (SSE-AMX), AArch64, RISC-V, PowerPC targets.
caveats: Paper does not give a code link for the DL primitives (they build on LIBXSMM's batch-reduce GEMM); numbers are vs 2019 MKL-DNN and small/medium sizes; compiler/flags not captured. LIBXSMM README itself has no oneDNN comparison.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ GEMM kernels outperform oneDNN MKL; follow-up of libxsmm repo

compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3.0, Ubuntu 18.04.5; oneMKL 2021.1 beta (flags in Makefile)
name: Optimizing DGEMM on Intel CPUs with AVX512F
workload: Double-precision GEMM serial and parallel, 19 stepwise kernels vs MKL at multiple matrix sizes.
claimed_speedup: Kernel 18 (serial) and 19 (parallel) 'reach the performance comparable to / faster than Intel MKL' on latest Intel CPUs; peak single core 128 GFLOPS (exact ratios are in plots, not quoted)
tradeoffs: AVX512F only, DGEMM only, inline assembly; GPL-3.0.
caveats: Tutorial-style; win vs MKL is 'comparable' on one CPU and old MKL beta; exact flags live in Makefile not read. Tier A is borderline because flags were not read. Baseline is MKL, not oneDNN.

name: Fastor
workload: Small fixed-size tensor/matrix operations and tensor-network contractions with compile-time operation minimisation.
claimed_speedup: README claims 'performance on par with MKL JIT's dedicated API' and shows plots where FLOP-optimal contraction ordering beats single-expression evaluation (no numbers read)
tradeoffs: Header-only, fixed-size tensors only, no dynamic allocation; compile-time cost for large expressions.
caveats: Numbers appear only in plots on the README/wiki, none extracted; benchmark compares against Eigen in the wiki but this was not opened. Low confidence on the speedup claim.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ header-only tensor library faster than Eigen Tensor benchmark contraction

name: TCL (Tensor Contraction Library)
baseline: Eigen Tensor, Tensor Toolbox, NumPy, ITensor
workload: 1000 random tensor contractions on 24 threads (TTGT-based contraction).
claimed_speedup: Speedup over the best reference among Eigen, Tensor Toolbox, NumPy and ITensor, 'reaching up to 18x' for low arithmetic intensity contractions
tradeoffs: Depends on HPTT transposition library; dual LGPL-3.0/GPL-3.0; unmaintained, author points to NVIDIA cuTensor.
caveats: Speedup is vs the best of several references, per-library numbers not given on the page; old hardware; abandoned.

name: MNN
baseline: TensorFlow Lite, TensorFlow, PyTorch Mobile, TVM
workload: Mobile/edge CNN inference latency using hand-written ARM/x86 assembly, Winograd and FP16 kernels; scripts in /benchmark.
claimed_speedup: 'Twice speed increase for new architecture ARM v8.2 with FP16 half-precision'; benchmark scripts compare against TF/TFLite/PyTorch/TVM, detailed results in OSDI'22 Walle paper (numbers not extracted)

hardware: Apple M4 Pro (CPU numbers); GPU model not captured
name: nanoinfer (int8 GEMM vs cuBLAS)
workload: Hand-written CUDA int8 GEMM (WMMA + shared memory) vs cuBLAS at n=256..4096; CPU conv engine vs ONNX Runtime on Apple M4 Pro.
claimed_speedup: CUDA int8 GEMM ahead of cuBLAS (NN layout) up to n=1024, e.g. 2.09x at n=256, but about 30% behind at 2048+; README itself says cuBLAS TN path is 1.6x-4.5x faster than the hand kernel at every size. CPU engine at parity with ONNX Runtime on dense models (e.g. MNIST 49 us vs 48 us), 1.3-1.7x slower on depthwise
tradeoffs: Educational engine; int8 path adds latency on AMX-equipped hardware.
caveats: Win over cuBLAS only holds for the row-major (NN) call layout and small n; the author concedes it vanishes against cuBLAS TN. CPU side is not faster than ONNX Runtime. Included as flagged/weak evidence only.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ neural network inference kernels faster than oneDNN XNNPACK benchmark github
